Transcript block 1 (source interval 000000-000299 seconds):
[00:00:00.612] Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry. We will continue with module 7 on functional materials on polymers, and today we are going to study about adhesives and specifically about epoxy resin.
[00:00:15.460] Let us first define adhesives, yes, substances which are used to bind two or more materials firmly by surface attachment due to the penetration of the adhesive into the material and solidification which leads to interfacial locking.
[00:00:32.624] So, when we have two surfaces and we apply the liquid adhesive onto the surface and bring them together, what exactly happens is the adhesive is going to penetrate into the top layers of the two surfaces, and then it is going to
[00:00:49.040] uh bind together by a solidification process. Only when it solidifies then the two surfaces get locked to each other.
[00:00:59.108] So there could be natural adhesives, we are all aware, of gum, glue, starch, etc., or there are many synthetic adhesives also available these days. The examples would be phenol formaldehydrasen, urea formal dehydration, and epoxytes.
[00:01:14.756] How do these actually work? Now adhesives are basically low molecular weight polymers which are dissolved in a solvent.
[00:01:25.508] After that, the most important step is to add a curing agent. What does this curing agent do? It is going to trigger cross-linking into the adhesive.
[00:01:39.536] And because of cross-linking three-dimensional network which is formed, solidification happens, and what you get is a thermoset solid polymer, and that is how the two surfaces got bound together. So there are two parts always in an
[00:01:54.864] Addition one is the low molecular weight polymer, which is soluble, and the other one, which we usually refer to as hardener, is actually known as a curing agent, and that is responsible for the uh solidification of the
[00:02:11.428] Polymer and that happens due to three-dimensional cross-linking network getting form. Now
[00:02:19.024] There are certain materials for which you have to use a particular type of adhesive. For example, for rubber we use phenol formaldehydrin. For wood, it's usually urea formalhydrasin, but epoxy resin is a very very good resin because.
[00:02:36.688] because it can be used to attach metal, wood, glass, concrete, leather, any kind of surfaces, epoxy resin can act as a very good adhesive.
[00:02:50.436] So let us study in more detail about what exactly is there in the structure of epoxy resin that is making it so effective as an adhesive. So basically, as we know from the name, there is an epoxy group. What is an epoxy group? It is a three-membered ring.
[00:03:07.376] of an O atom bonded to carbon atoms. So when we have three member ring, we know that this is going to be very very reactive.
[00:03:18.372] Three member rings are usually very reactive. Now this epoxy resin is commercially available to us in the form of araldite or epon. Let us see the synthesis.
[00:03:29.728] Now when you want to make an epoxy resin, it is a condensation reaction which will take place between bisphenol A and epichlorohydrate. So before we talk about the condensation between the two monomers.
[00:03:43.696] Let us see how to synthesize these monomers in the first place. Now, bisphenol A is the first monomer which is being used. Now, bisphenol, the name itself suggests there are two phenol groups and A stands for acetone.
[00:03:57.520] So two phenol molecules and one acetone molecule. When these react, what we get is the bisphenol A.
[00:04:07.108] The other monomer is epi chloroth. Now in epichlorohydrate we start with propene and we are going to chlorinate it. We add Cl2, what we get is the allyl chloride.
[00:04:22.052] That is now treated with HOCl. So this is now going to give you 13 dichloro 2 propanol or 12 dichloro 1 propanol. Now in this case, once now you do uh treat it with the base, what will happen is
[00:04:39.520] Dehydration is going to happen. It's sorry, it's Cl will be removed, and you get a three-membered ring over there. So one of them will be now it will become this three-membered ring, and you have the
[00:04:52.960] uh Cl over here. So this is known as Epichlorohydrine and you get NaCl because you are treating with it NaOH NaOH plus this HCl so you get the NaCl. So this is how epi chlorohydrine is made.

Transcript block 2 (source interval 000300-000599 seconds):
[00:05:09.696] So we are the starting point would be probene, or sometimes we say with the starting point is ally chloride. Now that we have learned the synthesis of the monomers bisphenol A and epi chlorohydrate, let us see how we synthesize the epoxy resin.
[00:05:27.268] So we have taken this epichlorohydrate and this is the this phenol A. And what do we notice here that there is an OH group over here and a Cl.
[00:05:38.464] So we know that they can be condensed easily. These two molecules can undergo condensation, and this would happen in the presence of NaOH. So when NaOH is used,
[00:05:50.272] HCl is getting eliminated. So there will be an HCl molecule which is getting removed here. And what would happen as a result of this condensation? We can see here that there is an attachment between the bisphenol A and
[00:06:06.560] And the epi chlorhydrate. So this molecule has basically condensed with this molecule with the elimination of HCl, but something else has also happened. This ring has opened up because if you look at this monoma.
[00:06:21.380] There are two hydroxyl groups on both sides, therefore it would classify as a monomalase. In the first class I mentioned, at least two functional groups should be there. But in this epiclorohydrate, we find there is just one CL which can take part in the condensation, whereas here we don't find anything, but yes.
[00:06:39.168] That is the reason why we have the ring here. Now this ring being very reactive, it is going to open up when this
[00:06:48.768] uh uh condensation will happen and therefore this ring is going to open up like this and we will find that we get the ch oh you can see here the ch oh is formed and now this ch2 is free to condense with the next
[00:07:06.224] bisphenol A ring. So this is how the condensation goes on. So between the two one side uh both of these will take part in the condensation. So the repeat unit is going to be the bisphenol A and this and this is the mechanism by which it happens.
[00:07:23.920] So here now this we have Cl condensation on one side and the other side it is CH2 where the ring is opened up and there's a free bond here that is going to react with the next bisphenol A. So this is the mechanism, and therefore we get this as the
[00:07:40.036] main uh repeat unit in the epoxy uh polymer. Now an important fact which we have to know that whenever a this
[00:07:51.104] Epoxy resin is formed, an excess of epichlorohydrine is used. What would be the reason for that? The reason is that the N groups we want them to be epoxy groups. Now, how would we
[00:08:04.880] Uh make sure that the uh that happens by using an excess of epi chlorohyain. When we use excess of epichlorohyden, because there is no more bisphenol, further reaction with bisphenole is not possible. If there was more bisphenol as we understood the mechanism just now, this ring would open.
[00:08:22.512] We'll get a CHOH and the CH2 combined would have combined with another bisphenole, but there is no bisphenol, so the ring remains intact, and in the end, we have ensured that both the side chains, the end of terminal chains, terminal groups are epoxy groups. So why would we do
[00:08:40.080] That because we know that epoxy is a very reactive group, and when we add the curing agent, immediately there will be a
[00:08:51.204] Three dimensional cross link structure which is formed, and we know that when between these two chains we have cross-link structure getting formed, the polymer is going to solidify. So that is the reason why we use excess of epiclorohydrate, and of course, curing agents, what are we going to
[00:09:08.976] Use we use diamines, di carboxylic acid, or acid anhydrides. So using these curing agents.
[00:09:16.688] Because there are these reactive epoxy groups, immediately cross link structure will be formed, which will result in solidification, and hence the two surfaces are going to get bound. So this is how the
[00:09:31.088] uh synthesis of epoxy resin is done and this is how it works in binding those two surfaces together. What are the properties of these epoxy resins?
[00:09:44.420] They have, of course, excellent addition, excellent resistance to water, acid, alkali, and other corrosive chemicals. So they are extremely resistant. And they also have very high mechanical strength. They absorb less moisture.

Transcript block 3 (source interval 000600-000899 seconds):
[00:10:00.880] and they have very good insulation properties. So they have wonderful properties, epoxy resins have very good properties and they're all listed here. Now what would be the applications for these epoxy resins?
[00:10:16.464] Now cured epoxy resins are frequently used in aerospace and defense. They are also used to bind glass, metal, leather, wood, ceramic, etc. Of course, that is the uh reason why they come under the class of adhesives. Then when they are coated on the floor, they give
[00:10:34.096] and anti-skid layer. They are used for laminating materials and for crease and shrinkage resistance in fabric. So that is why epoxy resin acts as a very good adhesive.
[00:10:51.524] So in the next class we are going to talk of another important class of polymers or rather polymer composites. So we will take up Kepler in the next class. Thank you.
